content:
I've been starting to revamp mk_all to prepare for making it more generally usable downstream (#45108). Specifically, I'm setting up a persistent Config which a package could (in the future) store in json, and which allows specifying all of the behavior Mathlib needs in a generic form, so that Mathlib does not need to be special-cased in mk_all. (It also integrates it more closely with Lake functionality, which is already available but not used.)

However, I'm realizing that the ergonomics could use some polishing.

Creation behavior

There are two potentially distinct roles mk_all has:

  1. generate aggregate files (from folders) that did not previously exist
  2. keep aggregate files up-to-date

Currently, it simply does both. But this means that we need config exceptions to avoid generating files for MathlibTest and Cache.

My suggestion here would be to change the behavior so that we need --generate (or --init?) to create aggregate files that did not yet exist, and by default we only update aggregate files that already exist and respect the lack of aggregate files elsewhere. This means we would not need a config exception for MathlibTest when merely updating the aggregate files in CI. (Pseudoroots like Mathlib.Tactic would of course be insisted upon.)

What do people think about this change? How heavily is the creation behavior integrated into CI workflows, and would this break anything? (Note: we could, of course, also use a different name in order to soft-deprecate mk_all—mk_all is nice and short but maybe not very specific.)

Output form

mk_all also demands that the entire aggregate file is just the imports. But I think it would be reasonable for people to want:

a. content after the imports such as commands
b. copyright headers and comments in line with the imports

A feature we might want, then, is to only modify the header while preserving subsequent commands, and to do so in a way that respects inline comments/copyright headers. (We have the infrastructure for this now in import-graph, by the way; we'd just need to integrate it)

I thought it's worth asking: does anyone downstream have a use case for mk_all preserving comments or commands after imports like this? (If not, this is maybe not so important.)

Git behavior

I believe most people use git, but currently the default of mk_all is to not use git (it's hidden behind the --git flag). This puts gitignored scratch files in aggregators by default. (As an anecdote, I didn't know --git existed for the longest time and just didn't use mk_all. I think I've heard of at least one other person who didn't know about this too.)

Would it be reasonable to have git be the default, check if the repo is a git repo, and further, insist on --no-git if it is not a git repo? After all, this suggests that the user may not be using version control, and so I think it might be good to verify that they actually want this program to overwrite their unversioned files! :)

Exit code shenanigans

This is minor, but I thought I should ask here. Currently the script hijacks the exit code to report the number of files that were changed by mk_all. The justification given in a comment is that we can then use this value further in CI. But, as far as I can see(?) we only use it to determine whether an update is needed or not (i.e. whether it's nonzero) in which case using exit codes as intended would still work. Should we use more conventional exit code meanings or do we need the information on how many files we've updated somewhere?

Sounds good!

RE git: I think a common use-case is to run it after creating a file, but I think --git doesn't list untracked files, even if they're not ignored. Could we pass some flags to git ls-files so that it'd list all non-ignored files?
(it does currently list staged untracked files though)

RE creation: we just have to add a check in Mathlib's CI that all the expected aggregate files exist, just in case someone deletes one of them for some reason
Also worth noting that #44573 will make mk_all run in CI :octopus: (I don't think it needs any special fixes)

Snir Broshi said:

Could we pass some flags to git ls-files so that it'd list all non-ignored files?

Hmm, looks like maybe git ls-files --cached --others --exclude-standard? That seems to respect gitignore but include untracked files. (A little hazy on just how wide the scope of "others" is, though.)

A related issue is that I'm not sure how to exclude unstaged deleted files...I tried --no-deleted, but this doesn't seem to work.
Oh, wait, actually we filter out nonexistent files on the Lean side anyway, so that shouldn't be a problem. :)

Snir Broshi said:

RE creation: we just have to add a check in Mathlib's CI that all the expected aggregate files exist, just in case someone deletes one of them for some reason

Aha, good point!

Hmm, that actually suggests that "keeping things up-to-date" really means enforcing that the files which you want to be there are actually there. So this information should be part of the config after all and not automatically detected from the layout!

Maybe the safe approach therefore is to just be able to generate a config which matches your current layout.

So I suppose we do not need --generate after all. The commands are actually divided as "prepare aggregator updates given the config (plus the provided flags)" and "prepare the config given the current aggregator layout (plus the provided flags)". Then variations on what to do with that information (just report, overwrite files, etc.).

I am not entire sure whether this is an (implicit) part of your proposal, but I have thought for a bit about the following fundamental change to how mk_all is used in mathlib: instead of having all files imported in Mathlib.lean, every folder comes with a file of the same name that contains public import of all files within that folder. So for instance Mathlib/Analysis.lean contains public imports of Mathlib/Analysis/*.lean. By induction this implies that Mathlib.lean contains public imports of all files in any subfolder of Mathlib/ (extra points if mk_all contains a proof of this at some point).

The main downside of this proposal is that there will be quite a few new files, but I would argue that there are very strong upsides (especially if combined with the Output form proposal).

  • Importing downstream (or for development): currently you have the choice of either importing all of mathlib or the precisely files you need. The former has the problem that you import a lot of stuff that you will never use and the later has the problem that you might import not enough. If you can public import Mathlib.Analysis and public import Mathlib.NumberTheory for your analytic number theory project, that would be way more ergonomic.
  • Deprecation: one type of deprecation that we will never get rid of is splitting a file into several files. This would be a non-breaking change if original file continues to exist (as the imports) and the contents just move into a subfolder.
  • Documentation: with verso in the documentation, we could write more "overview" type documentation in the new files. In particular, we can document questions like "what goes where", and similar large scale design questions, that currently don't have a natural home

We'll have to move 95 files for this change before creating the new ones, since keeping both Foo.lean and Foo/ is a common pattern. For most of those you could move Foo.lean to Foo/Basic.lean, but 14 of those already have a Basic.lean.

For documentation there are various README.md files in some folders, so they do currently have a natural home. Although it's not Verso.

Is this useful in practice? e.g. how many imports in Cslib would this save? (I'd imagine it's not very common to import an entire folder)
Does Foo.lean usually import everything in Foo/ as things currently stand? Or, what purpose do they serve?
(FWIW if we do eventually do this I'd be happy to implement it, it sounds fairly straightforward :) )

I also wonder if we'd want to curate a list of folders that should have this behavior. Apparently ~640 folders have ≤ 4 *.lean files and no subdirectories. Should we really make one for all of them? I'd worry it would make navigating the file tree a little difficult. I think the mentioned benefits (which I agree are benefits) are mostly present only for larger folders, right? Or is there some benefit to making it uniform I'm not seeing?

Using markdown instead of verso seems to me like a way worse option. You don't get links to code, type-checking, LaTeX, etc. I would personally would not be motivated to either read or write markdown for documentation. The variation would be to have a Readme.lean in each folder, which would solve the documentation problem, but has no impact on the other points (a problem with that is that it is not stable under splitting files: you move the module doc-string to a new Readme.lean?)

Assuming that

Is this useful in practice?

refers to the imports: I think so, but obviously the question is what is your hardware. If you can easily run files with import Mathlib, then there is no difference to you. But again this is not very future proof.
In Is there code for X? people tend to import Mathlib. If you just import the minimal set of files for a theorem with sorries to compile, then that might be very inconvenient for someone helping. But on the other hand, some topology question will most likely not involve algebraic geometry.
Personally, I never use import Mathlib because on my machine I can feel the difference (and I definitively don't need algebraic geometry, category theory, etc), so I usually import a file, where I assume that its transitive imports cover what I need. This is not a great and I would love to have a better option (and also an option that I can tell students to use).
Could you provide examples of where this saves lots of imports without significant overhead? Perhaps in downstream libraries?

Thomas Murrills said:

Does Foo.lean usually import everything in Foo/ as things currently stand? Or, what purpose do they serve?

I clicked around and some of the files doing the opposite: the toplevel file gets imported by the leaf file (so more what a Basic file usually does). One example of both a Basic and a toplevel file is Mathlib/Topology/Order.lean and Mathlib/Topology/Order/Basic.lean.
I would just import Mathlib.Analysis in all of my projects. At the very least in all files where I still not sure what the minimal imports are (because the scope of the file is not fixes).
Out of the 95 non-deprecated Foo.leans that have a Foo/, 28 of them (transitively) import everything in the folder, and 59 of them import nothing from the folder.

Thomas Murrills said:

I also wonder if we'd want to curate a list of folders that should have this behavior. Apparently ~640 folders have ≤ 4 *.lean files and no subdirectories. Should we really make one for all of them? I'd worry it would make navigating the file tree a little difficult. I think the mentioned benefits (which I agree are benefits) are mostly present only for larger folders, right? Or is there some benefit to making it uniform I'm not seeing?

Yes, the tree would be worse and I agree the most bang for your buck is in the larger folders. Advantages of making it uniform is that the implementation of any check that everything is imported is very simple: for every folder Foo/ you check whether ../Foo.lean imports all Foo/*.lean files. Also if we declare a random size of folders, then it will be annoying to do the change at a random point in time (and not at folder creation time).
We could just go one level deeper: aggregators for all top-level folders in Mathlib/

I think one should either do all subfolders or just the top level ones like Snir suggested (which would be reasonable as long as Mathlib doesnt increase in size significantly IMO). Everthing else (like a custom curated list) could become tedious and I arbitrary I feel like

Hmmm, I'm not sure we can escape the arbitrariness, since that's just emergent from what is arbitrarily useful to humans! But the tedium we could avoid. :)

Here's a middle ground: we have a curated list of superaggregator folders. Every folder directly below a superaggregator gets an adjacent aggregator file. So, we get Snir's suggestion of going one level deep by declaring Mathlib a superaggregator. Then we can declare just a handful of folders within Mathlib to also be superaggregators. (Maybe each subfolder of, I don't know, Analysis also gets an aggregator file, by declaring Mathlib.Analysis a superaggregator?)

I'm guessing this is what the generic implementation would have to be like anyway, since of course not every root file would behave this way :)
I'm not keen on allowing any customization here (unnecessary complexity, and allowing bikeshedding), we should just be doing it for all folders (my preference) or all top-level folders.
Just curious, do you mind saying why you prefer all folders? (Asking mainly because that means a lot of new files to wade through in the file explorer :sweat_smile:)
Because it's simple and predictable and gives downstream users the choice what they want?
Ah, so, mainly for the folder importability feature, is what I'm getting at :) (As opposed to the project organization/documentation features also mentioned above, or something not yet mentioned)

A proposal from some time ago was that writing import <path> would

  • if <path> is a file, import it
  • if <path> is a dir, import all files contained in that dir.

Basically, Moritz's suggestion, but without having to create the files, just as a default fallback directly in core. What I liked about this proposal is that it removes the need to have these "import all" files.

I think we don't want mk_all to be too smart, indeed, and it would be good to (re)design it in such a way that it can be easily replaced with built-in Lean/Lake functionality. Damiano's suggestion would be very nice.
Maybe we should have an opt-in/-out switch in the Lakefile for which folders get a mk_all'd Lean file?

I would like to replace the Foo/README.md files with a Foo.lean with a good Verso doc that imports everything, or perhaps a curated subset. And I suppose the difficulty with mk_all is it might overwrite the curated subset with the whole set of Lean files in that directory. So having some mechanism to control which files get their imports updated seems good.

Snir Broshi said:

Is this useful in practice? e.g. how many imports in Cslib would this save? (I'd imagine it's not very common to import an entire folder)

Currently CSLib has narrow imports, but I guess the effect of these aggregator modules would depend on how you configure shake? The more mathematical downstream repos might be better to look at, especially if they don't use shake.

In general I'm fairly happy with the current mk_all downstream. Maybe I'd appreciate the --generate option, as we do have a CslibTests.lean file solely because mk_all creates it, but I'm mostly neutral on the other points.

I think I'd prefer if the script's output would be consistent regardless of what's in the file already or whether it exists. For example if there's merge conflicts in the file, I can just run the script and be confident that whatever mess git left in there will be fixed

Felix Pernegger said:

Apparently there are 119 such files right now

Indeed, but some of those are deprecated. See the numbers upthread (conflicting files & dirs, conflicting Basic.lean)
Ah thank, I guess I should have read the entire thread... :sweat_smile:

I've checked CSLib and I believe that with aggregators for everything they cannot save any imports.

So we still have the Verso argument for READMEs, and the RAM argument for adding just top-level folder aggregators, but I see no reasons for aggregators for everything unless the language itself supports it automatically.

I haven't read the entire discussion about what mathlib should do, just as a feature request for some other projects, it would be really nice if mk_all had the mentioned option with the intermediate files. Concretely, I would like

A.lean
A/
  B.lean
  B/
    C.lean
    D.lean
  E.lean
  E/
     F.lean

Then A.lean would only contain

public import B.lean
public import E.lean

as B.lean and E.lean are also autocreated and contain the folders content.

Ok, since it seems we want something one way or another, I've at least put the internal-refactoring PR (#45108) out for review, since I think that'll be easier to build any of our future functionality on. :)
